## Introduction

Standard area diagrams (SADs) are sets of images of diseased organs with known
severity that raters consult while estimating severity by eye. A new SAD is
usually validated by asking a group of raters to assess the same images
without and then with the SAD, and comparing the accuracy of the two sets of
estimates.

The `sad_*` functions of {r4pde} cover two ways of analysing such a study:

```text
sad_data()                         organise and check the estimates
   │
   ├── conventional, two stages
   │     sad_ccc()                 Lin's statistics per rater and condition
   │     sad_compare()             means and Tukey letters by condition
   │     sad_reliability()         ICC and OCC among raters
   │     sad_plots()               exploratory figures
   │
   └── one stage, hierarchical model
         sad_fit()                 mixed model of all estimates
         sad_curve()               bias, variance and expected error along severity;
                                   functional comparison of conditions
         sad_regions()             severity ranges where conditions differ
         sad_raters(), sad_images()  rater calibration and image difficulty
         sad_simulate()            power for planning a new study
```

The example uses `SADRustSoybean`, from the study of Franceschi et al. (2020).
Forty raters estimated the severity of soybean rust on 50 leaves without a SAD
and then with a SAD. Raters 1 to 20 used an old SAD and raters 21 to 40 a new
one. The design therefore compares two SADs, each against its own unaided
baseline.

```{r}
library(r4pde)
head(SADRustSoybean)
```

## Preparing the data

The estimates are in wide format, one column per method. `wide` names the
estimate columns, and its names become the method labels. `group` says which
SAD each rater used, so there are four conditions.

```{r}
x <- sad_data(SADRustSoybean, rater = "rater", image = "leaf", actual = "actual",
              wide = c(UN = "unaided", SAD = "aided"), group = "sad")
x
```

For a study with a single SAD, leave out `group`:

```{r}
x_new <- sad_data(subset(SADRustSoybean, sad == "New"),
                  wide = c(UN = "unaided", SAD = "aided"))
levels(x_new$condition)
```

## Conventional analysis

### Lin's concordance per rater

The first stage summarises each rater under each condition by Lin's
concordance correlation coefficient ($\rho_c$) and its components: precision
($r$), the bias correction factor ($C_b$), the scale shift ($v$) and the
location shift ($u$, negative when the rater underestimates).

```{r}
cc <- sad_ccc(x)
head(cc)
```

### Comparing conditions

The second stage compares the means of these statistics between conditions.
Because the same raters assessed the images without and with the SAD, a mixed
model with rater as random effect is used, followed by Tukey's test. The table
matches Table 2 of Franceschi et al. (2020).

```{r, eval = has_compare}
cmp <- sad_compare(x, cc)
cmp
```

### Inter-rater reliability

```{r}
sad_reliability(x)
```

### Exploratory plots

```{r, fig.height = 3}
p <- sad_plots(x, cc, baseline = "UN")
p$scatter
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.2}
p$box_ccc
```

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 3.5}
p$gain_vs_baseline
```

The new SAD improved agreement for every rater, while the old SAD helped some
raters and made others worse.

## One-stage hierarchical model

The two-stage analysis reduces 50 estimates per rater to a single number, and
cannot say at which severity a SAD helps. `sad_fit()` models all estimates at
once: each condition has its own bias and calibration slope, raters have their
own intercepts and slopes in each method, images have an intrinsic difficulty
and the residual variance changes with severity and condition.

```{r, eval = has_models}
fit <- sad_fit(x)
fit
```

`structure = "auto"` tries richer random-effects structures first and keeps the
first that converges.

### Bias and expected error along the severity range

`sad_curve()` turns the model into curves. With `reference = "UN"`, each SAD is
compared with the unaided estimates of the same raters, using simultaneous
confidence bands over the whole severity range.

```{r, eval = has_models}
cv <- sad_curve(fit, reference = "UN")
sad_regions(cv)
```

```{r, eval = has_models}
plot(cv, "bias")
plot(cv, "difference")
```

The old SAD shifted estimates downwards, and the shift grows with severity.
The new SAD did not change the bias significantly anywhere in the range. Its
benefit is precision, which shows in the expected absolute error, which
combines bias and the variation among raters, among images and within raters:

```{r, eval = has_models}
plot(cv, "expected_abs_error")
```

### A functional model for the error curves

`type = "smooth"` replaces the straight lines by smooth error curves, with a
random smooth curve per rater, fitted by `mgcv::bam()`. It shows where along
the severity range the two conditions differ, without assuming a linear bias.

```{r, eval = has_models}
cs <- sad_curve(fit, type = "smooth", reference = "UN")
sad_regions(cs)
plot(cs, "difference")
```

### Raters and images

```{r, eval = has_models, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
rt <- sad_raters(fit)
plot_sad_raters(rt)
```

```{r, eval = has_models}
head(sad_images(fit))
```

Images with large absolute difficulty were consistently over- or
underestimated by all raters and deserve a second look.

## Planning a new study

`sad_simulate()` estimates the power of the paired t test on $\rho_c$ and of
the likelihood ratio test of the one-stage model for a given number of raters
and images. Each scenario fits many models, so the call below is not run.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
sad_simulate(n_rater = c(10, 20), n_image = c(20, 40), nsim = 200,
             shift = -3, precision = 0.8, cores = 4)
```

## Reference

Franceschi, V. T., Alves, K. S., Mazaro, S. M., Godoy, C. V., Duarte, H. S. S.,
and Del Ponte, E. M. (2020). A new standard area diagram set for assessment of
severity of soybean rust improves accuracy of estimates and optimizes resource
use. Plant Pathology 69:495-505.
